title: Password Attacks: from wordlist to spraying
description: Wordlists, mangling rules, targeted vs online attacks, spraying and the NTLM world: the theory behind every cracked hash.

1.title: Wordlists and mangling rules
1.body:
## The raw material: wordlists

| Wordlist | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `rockyou.txt` (14M) | The universal starting point |
| `SecLists` (GitHub) | Meta-collection: by service, by language, patterns |
| `honeypot` / recent leaks | What attackers really use today |
| Generated (CUPP, mentha) | Aimed at ONE victim with a known profile |

```bash
# Kali ships rockyou gzipped:
sudo gunzip -d /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz

# CUPP: password for 'Alice Smith, from accounting, Barça fan, born 1990'
cupp -i
# → asmith1990, Barca1990!, Contabilidad2026...
```

The operational lesson: a targeted wordlist of 500 words against one specific
user usually beats the 14-million-word rockyou. Context
(LinkedIn, social media) multiplies effectiveness far beyond sheer volume.

## Rules: 14 million becomes billions

A rule transforms every word in the list: `Marcos` → `Marcos2026`,
`M4rc0s!`, `marcosmarcos`... The standard collections (`best64.rule`,
`dive.rule`) condense what people actually do with their
passwords:

```bash
# NTLM with rules — the command you will see in every AD engagement:
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule

# How many candidates does it generate? (estimation mode):
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule --stdout | wc -l
```

Order matters: first the good wordlist, then the good rules.
A leaked list from the sector + best64 beats any pure brute force
(which at 8 characters with symbols already takes centuries).

## The hashcat -m map

| -m | Hash | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | MD5 | Old apps, forums |
| 1000 | NTLM | Windows/AD (the star) |
| 1800 | sha512crypt | Linux /etc/shadow |
| 3200 | bcrypt | Modern apps |
| 13100 | Kerberoast TGS | AD service tickets |

`hashcat --example-hashes` lists all 300+. Identifying the format
BEFORE cracking is half the job (does it start with `$2y$`? bcrypt. `$krb5tgs`?
kerberoast).

password-attacks-t01-q01.prompt: What is THE 14-million-password wordlist shipped by default in Kali (/usr/share/wordlists/)?
password-attacks-t01-q01.hint: rockyou.txt (from the 2009 RockYou breach) — it ships gzipped: gunzip it once

password-attacks-t01-q02.prompt: Which tool generates personalized wordlists from the victim's profile (name, company, birthday, hobbies)?
password-attacks-t01-q02.hint: CUPP — it asks interactive questions and builds the tailored list

password-attacks-t01-q03.prompt: In hashcat, what are RULES applied to a wordlist?
password-attacks-t01-q03.hint: Think about what people do with their base password: capitalize, add the year... best64.rule is the standard collection.

options.a: Legal norms that limit which passwords may be tried
options.b: Filters that discard words that are too short from the wordlist
options.c: Transformations applied to every word in the wordlist (capitalize, suffixes, leetspeak)
options.d: Speed limits that protect the target hash

password-attacks-t01-q04.prompt: Write the hashcat command to crack an NTLM hash (/tmp/hash.txt) with rockyou + best64 rules on GPU.

2.title: Offline vs online: two different games
2.body:
## The fundamental difference

**Offline** (you have the hash): GPU speed (billions of
attempts/second on NTLM), no logs, no lockouts. The only wall is the real
length/complexity of the password.

**Online** (you talk to the service): network speed (~tens or
hundreds per second at best), WITH rate limiting, account
lockout, SOC alerts and captchas. The weakest password in the world
is useless if you lock the account before you find it.

```bash
# OFFLINE: hashcat all out (does not touch the target's network):
hashcat -m 1000 ntlm.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule

# ONLINE: hydra against SMB — SLOW and noisy:
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt 10.10.10.10 smb
```

## Spraying: the online tactic that actually works

Instead of `N passwords × 1 user` (guaranteed lockout), you do
`1 password × N users`, wait (hours, often) and repeat with
the next candidate. Seasonal passwords are the
perfect target:

```bash
# One spray round against the DC's SMB:
hydra -L users.txt -p "Verano2026!" 10.10.10.10 smb -t 4 -W 3
#  -t 4: 4 threads max (discretion)   -W 3: wait 3s between attempts

# Dedicated tool (more elegant with AD):
#     spray.sh or CrackerPack: calendars of common passwords
```

The typical lockout threshold (5-10 attempts) defines your rounds: 1 attempt
per account per day gets around almost any policy. That is why SIEMs
alert on "1 failure × 500 accounts" and not only on "500 failures × 1 account".

## Credential stuffing

The third mode, industrial: real username:password pairs from public
breaches (Collections, leaks) tried en masse against the target
login. It guesses nothing — it reuses. It is the definitive argument for
checking your corporate credentials against breach databases and
for 2FA on everything important.

## Defenses that really change the game

| Defense | Which attack it kills |
|---|---|
| Progressive lockout + delay | Online brute force |
| Spray detection (1 failure × many accounts) | Spraying |
| Breach-password screening (on-prem AD has it) | Stuffing and rockyou |
| 2FA/MFA | All of the above |
| bcrypt/argon2 + salt | Offline cracking (slows it down by orders of magnitude) |

password-attacks-t02-q01.prompt: What limits the speed of an ONLINE attack (against a real login) and does not exist in OFFLINE hash cracking?
password-attacks-t02-q01.hint: Offline only your GPU limits you; online there is a service defending itself.

options.a: The maximum length of the hash
options.b: The size of the wordlist, which is only used offline
options.d: Rate limit, account lockout and logs (countermeasures of the remote service)

password-attacks-t02-q02.prompt: What is the online attack that tries ONE password against MANY accounts instead of many against one?
password-attacks-t02-q02.hint: Password spraying — it avoids lockouts by staying under the per-account threshold

password-attacks-t02-q03.hint: It works because people reuse passwords across services.

options.a: Reusing credentials leaked in other breaches against the target login
options.b: Padding a wordlist with random passwords
options.c: Cracking hashes from an LSASS dump
options.d: Trying a single password against many accounts

password-attacks-t02-q04.prompt: In a hydra spray against the SMB of a DC (10.10.10.10), which strategy avoids account lockout?
password-attacks-t02-q04.hint: 1 attempt/user/round with pauses; in hydra: -L users.txt and a fixed password with -p, no -P.

options.a: Trying 1000 passwords against a single user as fast as possible
options.b: One attempt per user per round (fixed -p, no -P), with pauses between rounds
options.c: Launching as many threads as possible to finish before the lockout
options.d: Using only -P with the full wordlist against the administrator user

3.title: NTLM: the Windows hash world
3.body:
## Why NTLM rules in Windows engagements

Windows does not store your password: it stores `NTLM hash = MD4(UTF-16LE(
password))`. And the NTLM protocol authenticates by proving you know the
hash — not the password. Practical consequence: whoever steals the hash,
gets in. The typical chain:

```
phishing → shell as user → mimikatz/ProcDump of LSASS
→ NTLM hashes of the user (and of accounts/services in memory)
→ pass-the-hash to other machines → domain admin hash → game over
```

## Stealing the hashes

```powershell
# With an admin session on the target (classic tools):
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords     # dumps credentials from LSASS

# Without mimikatz (OPSEC): dump LSASS + crack offline:
procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp
# pypykatz lsass.dmp   → NTLM hashes on your machine
```

## Pass-the-hash in action

```bash
# Impacket — executive SMB with only the hash (empty LM : NTLM):
impacket-psexec.py -hashes :32ED87BDB5FDC5E9CBA88547376818D4 administrator@10.10.10.10

# Also: wmiexec.py, atexec.py, smbexec.py (same -hashes syntax)
```

The hash authenticates against SMB, WMI, WinRM... You only need the
plaintext password to crack the hash OFFLINE (hashcat -m 1000) when
you want to reuse it elsewhere (portals, VPN, email) where there
is no NTLM.

## The modern defense

- **Kerberos by default** in healthy domains: tickets are not derived from
  a reusable hash in the same way (attacks migrated to
  kerberoasting/tickets, not PtH).
- **Credential Guard** (VBS): isolates LSASS in a virtual enclave —
  classic mimikatz can no longer read it.
- **LAPS**: unique local admin passwords per machine, rotated —
  it kills the reuse that makes PtH scale.
- **No WDigest**, lsass protected process (`RunAsPPL`), and alerts for
  "local admin used on another machine".

The privesc-windows room (which you already did) and the active-directory-ataque room (the
grand finale of this path) practice several of these steps with labs; here remains the
theory that ties them together.

password-attacks-t03-q01.prompt: What is an NTLM hash and why can it be stolen from Windows memory (LSASS) even though the password is not there in plaintext?
password-attacks-t03-q01.hint: The derived value is enough to authenticate: the protocol only requires proving that you know the hash.

options.a: An AES encryption of the password that is decrypted with the domain key
options.b: A temporary Kerberos token that expires after 10 hours
options.c: The MD4 of the UTF-16LE of the password: Windows caches it to authenticate and the hash is enough
options.d: A copy of the plaintext password stored in the registry

password-attacks-t03-q02.prompt: What is the technique that uses the stolen NTLM hash itself to authenticate WITHOUT knowing the password?

password-attacks-t03-q03.prompt: Which Impacket tool runs commands on remote Windows given only user + NTLM hash?
password-attacks-t03-q03.hint: impacket-psexec.py -hashes :NTLM user@host (the Impacket suite: psexec, wmiexec, smbexec)

password-attacks-t03-q04.prompt: Which modern replacement for NTLM makes pass-the-hash useless by using cryptographic tickets?
password-attacks-t03-q04.hint: Kerberos (TGT/TGS) — that is why modern attacks go after tickets (kerberoasting) and cached credentials
